newsitem.title: UK: China says would use own reserves to defend HKG $.
newsitem.headline: China says would use own reserves to defend HKG $.

text.p: A senior Chinese official on Tuesday confirmed his country's commitment to the Hong Kong dollar peg and said China would be prepared to use its own currency reserves to defend it after the handover.
Deputy governor of the People's Bank of China, Chen Yuan, also pledged that China would not do anything to jeopardise Hong Kong's prosperity after it takes over next year.
"We...stand ready to use our foreign reserves to support the Hong Kong dollar if necessary," he said in a speech prepared for delivery at a seminar organised by the Bank of England.
"The People's Bank of China will support the currency stability of Hong Kong," Chen said.
Beijing was prepared to offer liquidity to support the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, which he inisisted would be answerable only to the Hong Kong government, to keep the dollar stable.

"I would like to stress that China supports Hong Kong's commitment to the maintenance of the linked exchange rate system, which has served Hong Kong well by providing monetary stability since its introduction in 1983."
The monetary authorities of Hong Kong and China will be mutually independent though they would have to increase cooperation.

Chen dismissed suggestions that Beijing would not honour its agreements after it takes over Hong Kong, whose role as a financial centre for China as well as Asia in general he saw as becoming even more important.
"It is...vital that Hong Kong remain the vibrant financial centre with its own economic system that we know now.
"We certainly would not do anything which would jeopardise Hong Kong's prospects," Chen said.
Speculation that Shanghai would replace Hong Kong as an international financial centre was groundless, he said.
"In the short run, and at least before the renminbi becomes fully convertible, it is not possible for Shanghai to become an international financial centre."
Chen said that given the size of China there was room for more than one financial centre and said the two would complement each other.
Hong Kong would remain prosperous after 1997 because of its strong economic fundamentals, legal safeguards ensuring continued stability and the economic development of the mainland, Chen added.
